data.title: European shares stumble at end of best month since June on AI worries
data.description:
Key points:
  • Bayer gains after winning Roundup cancer trial brought by three women
  • Universal Music rises as Q3 subscription streaming revenue improves
  • Euro zone economic growth surpasses expectations

By Avinash P and Niket Nishant

European shares dropped on Friday, hammered by a global tech selloff that shaved billions off the market values of some chip heavyweights, ending a largely strong month on a sour note.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index closed 0.36% lower at 646.75 points, despite recording its best month since June.

Results from Amazon and Intel in the US rekindled concerns about the high costs of building out AI infrastructure and prompted a pullback from technology names worldwide.

"The message from investors is becoming clearer: strong AI demand is no longer enough on its own," Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, said.

The European technology sector index (.SX8P) fell 2.75% for its worst day since July 7 and led sectoral declines. AT&S , Soitec and Technoprobe led losses on the STOXX 600, with declines ranging from 9% to 13%.

Robust earnings in Europe this quarter have offered some support to stocks, but the drop on Friday shows how quickly bullishness can evaporate if global sentiment shifts.

"The market is trying to wrestle with the equation. A huge amount of capex is being spent, relative to the timeline of a return on investment. And at the moment, they don't have an answer to that," Michael Hewson, chief analyst at MCH Market Insights, said.

GROWTH DEFIES HEADWINDS

Separately, data showed the euro zone economy grew faster than predicted last quarter, displaying exceptional resilience to headwinds from expensive energy, even as surging borrowing costs and rapid inflation cloud the outlook.

Additionally, French consumer prices rose more than expected in October, recording the highest inflation rate since December 2023.

Investors are already grappling with political unrest in the euro zone's second-largest economy, at a time when the country faces mounting pressure from elevated government debt, driving French bond yields to multi-year highs.

Universal Music Group jumped 7.89%, topping the STOXX 600, after posting a pick-up in subscription streaming revenue in the third quarter. The media sector (.SXMP) rose 1.63%.

BP rose marginally after posting third-quarter net income ahead of expectations, while German sportswear maker Puma advanced 5.59% after a quarterly sales beat.

Sanofi gained 4.71% after the French pharmaceutical firm reported third-quarter results ahead of analyst expectations and lifted its outlook.

Among other movers, Bayer gained 5.46% after winning a trial on Thursday over claims by three women that its Roundup weedkiller caused their cancer.

data.title: Spanish groups lead Brazil power transmission auction, committing $1.6 billion
data.description:
Spanish power companies Celeo, Cymi, Cox Energy and Iberdrola dominated a power transmission auction in Brazil on Friday, winning seven of eight projects to expand and strengthen the South American country's power grid.

The Brazilian units of the Spanish groups committed an estimated 8.56 billion reais ($1.59 billion) in investments, out of the auction's total 8.9 billion reais.

  • Celeo won the largest project in the auction, which is set to require 4.1 billion reais in investments to improve electricity service in Mato Grosso do Sul state

  • The company also won a project in Rondonia state with some 753 million reais in planned investments

  • Cymi secured a project in Sao Paulo state for about 1.1 billion reais in planned investments and another in Parana state worth 982.5 million reais

  • Neoenergia, controlled by Iberdrola, won projects in Bahia and Paraiba states totaling 1.16 billion reais in investments

  • Cox secured a lot worth 480 million reais in investments in Parana state

  • Portugal's EDP closed the winners' list with a project between Goias and Bahia states worth 317 million reais in investments

data.title: Coinbase's Profit Beat Comes With a Major Catch
data.description:
Coinbase shares fell nearly 7% in premarket trading Friday after investors looked past a headline profit beat and focused instead on weaker core revenue and plans by top executives to sell up to $2.2 billion of stock.

The crypto exchange reported third-quarter net income of $718.7 million, or $2.51 per diluted share, easily beating Wall Street expectations for a loss of about $0.15 per share.

But almost all of that profit came from a $715 million unrealized gain on Coinbase's crypto holdings, making the underlying operating picture much less impressive.

Core trading activity weakened sharply.

Total revenue fell 35% year over year to $1.22 billion, while transaction revenue dropped 44% to $590 million. Consumer spot trading volume sank 59%, and operating income from the exchange business fell to $61.7 million from $480.5 million a year earlier.

There were some bright spots.

CEO Brian Armstrong said prediction markets have now surpassed $200 million in annualized revenue, helping offset part of the weakness in spot trading.

Still, insider selling plans added another layer of pressure.

Armstrong, co-founder Fred Ehrsam and President Emilie Choi have filed Rule 10b5-1 plans covering up to 13.6 million shares over roughly 14 months, worth about $2.2 billion at Thursday's closing price. That represents around 6% of Coinbase's Class A shares.

Armstrong alone plans to sell up to 8.17 million shares, more than double the size of his prior plan. The company still has about $1.96 billion of authorized share repurchases available.

Investor Takeaway

I think the biggest issue here is that Coinbase's headline profit looks much stronger than the underlying business.

The company made more than $700 million, but almost all of that came from a mark-to-market crypto gain rather than the exchange itself.

That matters because transaction revenue is still the clearest read on Coinbase's core trading economics, and a 44% decline is difficult to ignore.

The insider-sale plans make the setup even more sensitive because they introduce the possibility of meaningful additional share supply while the stock is already well below its 52-week high.

For investors, the key things to watch are spot trading volumes, transaction revenue, prediction-market growth, insider Form 4 filings, and whether the company uses its buyback authorization aggressively enough to offset new supply.

Coinbase beat on profit.

But the quality of that profit is the real story.

data.title: Quess Corp Q2 Results: Net profit jumps 45% on staffing growth; declares ₹5 dividend
data.description:
Staffing and workforce solutions provider Quess Corp Ltd on Friday (October 30) reported a 44.9% year-on-year increase in net profit to ₹75 crore for the second quarter of FY27, compared with ₹52 crore in the year-ago period.

Revenue rose 14.7% to ₹4,396 crore from ₹3,832 crore, while earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) increased 11.6% to ₹86 crore from ₹77 crore. EBITDA margin remained flat at 2%.

The company declared an interim dividend of ₹5 per equity share, representing 50% of the face value of ₹10 per share, for FY27. November 6, 2026, has been fixed as the record date for determining shareholder eligibility. The dividend will be paid on or before November 20, 2026.

Quess Corp reported net cash of ₹471 crore and its highest-ever quarterly cash collection of more than ₹5,000 crore.

H1 FY27 Performance

For the first half of FY27, revenue stood at ₹8,578 crore, up 15% year-on-year. Adjusted EBITDA increased 22% to ₹178 crore, with the margin improving by 12 basis points year-on-year. Profit after tax (PAT) rose 53% to ₹157 crore, with earnings per share (EPS) at ₹10.4.

Return on equity (ROE) expanded to 25% from 20% in FY26, based on trailing 12-month PAT.

Q2 Segmental Performance

The General Staffing business reported revenue of ₹3,823 crore and EBITDA of ₹57 crore during the quarter. Its headcount stood at 490,000, with more than 20,000 additions. The business added 116 new contracts during the quarter.

The construction vertical's EBITDA nearly doubled year-on-year, with double-digit margins.

In Professional Staffing, margins stood at around 11%. Global Capability Centres (GCCs) contributed 71% of both headcount and revenue, with Banking, Financial Services and Insurance (BFSI) and CRT emerging as the leading growth verticals. The business added 27 new contracts.

Overseas Business

Quess Corp's overseas business added 33 new contracts and reported double-digit growth in both revenue and EBITDA.

The Middle East business maintained strong margins despite flat sequential revenue growth amid the geopolitical crisis. Singapore added eight new contracts, while Malaysia recorded 50% year-on-year revenue growth.

The Philippines business reported 15% year-on-year revenue growth, with a net margin of 10.5%.

Lohit Bhatia, ED and Group CEO, said, "We are pleased to report a good result for Q2, with revenue growing by 15% YoY to ₹4,396 crore and adj. EBITDA rising by 20% YoY to ₹92 crore. Our PAT and EPS grew 44% YoY, reaching ₹75 crore and ₹5, respectively, while delivering a ROE of 25%.

The Board has approved an interim dividend of ₹5 per share, reaffirming our commitment to creating sustainable value for our shareholders. This quarter’s performance was marked by a significant milestone as our headcount crossed 500k, driven largely by headcount additions of over 20k in our General Staffing business.

The segment delivered robust performance, adding 116 new client logos and achieving 15% YoY revenue growth and 23% YoY EBITDA growth, positioning us strongly for the quarters ahead. Professional Staffing recorded 13% YoY revenue growth, supported by sustained hiring demand from Global Capability Centres (GCCs).

Despite geopolitical challenges in the Middle East, our Overseas Business maintained momentum, delivering 10% YoY revenue growth and 23% YoY EBITDA growth. This performance was driven by higher margins in the Middle East, while Malaysia, Singapore, and the Philippines contributed to revenue growth.

On the people front, Quess was recognised among the Best Workplaces in the Middle East 2026, ranking 40th overall and 32nd among the Best Workplaces for Women in the Middle East, reinforcing our commitment to building an inclusive and empowering workplace."

Shares of Quess Corp Ltd ended at ₹306.95, down by ₹17.50, or 5.39%, on the BSE.

data.title: ServiceNow Plunges as Slower Growth Exposes Valuation Risk
data.description:
Enterprise workflow software provider ServiceNow Inc. (NOW, Financials) saw its valuation reset by 31% as investors fixated on slower subscription growth and deteriorating margins amid good sales growth.

Third quarter subscription revenue rose 20.5% at constant currency to $3.99 billion, total revenue was $4.11 billion.

The company's first quarterly profits shortfall in six quarters, with adjusted earnings of $1 per share falling 2 cents short of Wall Street expectations. More disturbing was the future.

Management estimates current remaining performance obligations growth of 18.5% in the fourth quarter, down from 21% in the third quarter. It also gave subscription revenue projection that was roughly $110 million short of what analysts had expected.

However, GAAP operating margin decreased to 9.5% from over 17% a year ago on higher infrastructure investment and acquisition integration costs.

That combination was a tough pill to swallow with the company selling around 68 times trailing earnings before the selloff.

Paycom is the exception. The smaller provider of HR software boasts gross margins of 88%, is forecasting full year free cash flow of more than $650 million and has been actively buying back its own shares.

The next catalyst is if ServiceNow can stabilize cRPO growth and reestablish profitability without compromising AI investment.

  • Banks (.FTNMX301010) weighed most on the index on Friday after NatWest lost nearly 9% following a weaker-than-expected outlook for interest income

  • Precious and industrial (.FTNMX551020) metal miners lost 5.3% and 2.9%, respectively, tracking declines in gold and copper

  • BP rose 0.5% after posting a record quarterly net profit

  • Earlier this week, finance minister John Healey's first budget raised taxes on banks and gambling firms by less than expected, sparking a rally in the stocks

  • Aerospace and defence firms were among the best performers this week after Healey said that 'reprioritisation' in other departments would fund the government's defence plan

  • Consumer staples stocks rose on the day, with British American Tobacco and Unilever up 1.7% and 2.1%

  • Earlier this month, data showed inflation rose more than expected in September, cementing the case for an interest rate hike by the Bank of England in November

data.title: What Does the Weil Gotshal Implosion Mean for the Law-Firm Industry? — WSJ
data.description:
By Erin Mulvaney and Andrew Scurria

The turmoil at Weil, Gotshal & Manges has led its leaders to wind down the law firm. They took the steps as the firm hemorrhaged top lawyers and had no clear succession plan after its incoming chair declined to step into the role.

As of Friday the would-be chair and a top private equity lawyer, Ramona Nee, was in talks to join Kirkland & Ellis, a massive rival with which Weil had struggled to compete.

Such a fall is extraordinary for a firm with some 1,200 lawyers worldwide and had been among the most well-regarded and profitable in the industry.

Despite its woes, Weil raked in $2.1 billion in revenue last year and, like most law firms, it has relatively few liabilities outside of its global office leases.

Here's what to know about the demise of one of Wall Street's most vaunted law firms and what happens now.

What triggered Weil's misfortunes?

The roots of the crisis at Weil date back more than a decade. The firm raked in business during the chaotic aftermath of the 2008-09 financial crisis but failed to reinvest those profits and even cut lawyers when many of its competitors were in growth mode. It has fallen behind industry leaders in head count, revenue and profit — leaving it vulnerable to poaching from rival firms.

Weil has pushed hard in the past year or so to grow, seeking a firm with which to merge and amping up efforts to lure new partners. Some firm insiders say there was a power struggle between influential partners who wanted to grow to compete with mega-firm rivals and others who wanted to remain smaller. In March, the firm elected private-equity partner Ramona Nee to take over leadership in January 2027. Nee recently decided to walk away from the role.

In September, news broke that Michael Aiello, the firm's top dealmaker, was leaving for Cravath, Swaine & Moore. It marked an inflection point. Efforts soon accelerated to find a merger partner. When a deal with Willkie Farr fell through and more top lawyers announced their departure, confidence in Weil's future cratered.

"A law firm's most valuable asset is its people. If they go home one night and don't come back the next day, it's over," said Albert Togut, a bankruptcy lawyer who handled the infamous collapse of Dewey & LeBoeuf.

What does the dissolution of a huge law firm mean for the industry?

In addition to Nee, many of the firm's partners, including Matt Barr, the head of Weil's prized restructuring practice, are being heavily courted by rivals. Barr is expected to stay at the firm to oversee the wind down. Landing those lucrative practice groups is crucial for firms who are in a race for top talent and scale.

The firm also has hundreds of associates who will be flooding the job market. Hiring at big law firms typically follows a rigid schedule, with firms beginning to interview future associates as early as their first semester of law school and making final hiring decisions before they begin their final year. That creates challenges for the roughly 100 Weil first-year associates looking for jobs outside of that timeline.

The whole legal industry is a bit chaotic right now. What's going on?

The partner exodus at Weil reflects upheaval in the legal industry as firms compete fiercely for top talent. Even healthy firms with strong reputations can be destabilized if they lose key people or practice groups.

It was once unusual for partners to jump from firm to firm, but in the current market, some of the most successful firms have amassed so much money that they can lure partners with $20 million-plus guarantees.

Unlike people in other industries, lawyers aren't bound by noncompete agreements, making lawyers free agents — and when they leave, they often take their prized clients with them.

Why is it shocking that Weil finds itself in crisis?

Weil, a white-shoe firm founded nearly a century ago by Jewish lawyers who were often excluded from other elite shops, has established itself as a blue-chip restructuring powerhouse with a strong record of clinching private equity and M&A deals. The firm was a pioneer in building a restructuring practice, leading some of the largest bankruptcies in history, including those of Lehman Brothers, General Motors and Enron.

Its financial picture has been healthy. Its partners earned $5.6 million each last year, making it one of the top 20 most profitable firms. But while partner profit at the top 100 firms grew 14% last year, Weil's grew only 4%.

How will Weil Gotshal wind down its financial affairs?

While some collapsing law firms have filed for chapter 11, Weil at this point is planning to wind down its affairs without a bankruptcy filing. Even as a shell of its former self, the firm is likely to continue to exist in some form for an extended time to manage the tasks of settling its accounts receivable, dealing with leases at offices around the world and administering payments to employees and partners.

Other firms hobbled by partner defections have wound down without the expense of a bankruptcy proceeding, including the restructuring and transactional boutique Stroock & Stroock & Lavan in 2023. Although Weil's affairs are more complex, the firm enters wind-down in a relatively strong financial position, with few liabilities and no debt. But it isn't clear how much of the firm's outstanding bills it will be able to collect or on what timeline.
